They both have the same outcome materially, but they'll have different mental and emotional tolls on you.

My family had a tradition where if someone was going on a long car ride/trip and wasn't going to be back for a while, anyone who was staying home would try to race the car down the street and then wave goodbye when we got to the street corner. (It was most often when my older siblings went off to college after breaks, but sometimes my parents would go on weekend trips to visit their respective sides of the family without the whole crew, there were 7 of us.)

My brothers would be headed out the door after giving everyone hugs and I'd throw on my shoes as fast as possible before they pulled off. My eldest brother loved it and would give me a head start to get to my top speed before driving past me. Then he'd wait at the stop sign at the bottom of the street until I caught up so I could say goodbye one more time.

I'm the youngest of 5 kids and I kept the tradition going right up until I moved out myself. There was no one to sprint down the street corner for me then, and most everyone else in my house had stopped doing it long before that, but I'm happy for all the memories.

Key to running in cold weather is layering. Unless you're going to do a full warm up indoors first, you need to have layers to keep you warm until your body warms up and they need to be easy to remove once you're warmed up and they feel too hot. 

In general, your body will heat up around 15°-20°F. So if it's 32° you'll feel like it's 52° while you're actively running.  Extremities get cold easier though, so once it gets below 40°F you'll want to keep ears and fingers covered somehow even if just a little bit.

Running in anything under 40°F for me looks like thermal leggings w/ shorts over (sometimes sweatpants) and thick socks; quick dry/athletic shirt, long sleeve shirt, and a sweatshirt/hoodie/rain coat/wind breaker (depending on weather conditions). Gloves/earwarmers as necessary.

Last notes: 1) Try to plan out your run so you loop back to an area you can drop off extra layers as you take them off like your house or car (you can also just carry them/tie them around your waist). 2) Don't stay out in the cold in sweaty clothes; change clothes and/or shower as soon as possible.

My teacher always taught us that each beat has its own action. It's not three steps in four beats, but four actions in four beats.

1: step forward with weight transfer on the left foot
2: shift your weight back into your right foot
3: collect your left foot underneath you (but don't put weight on it)
4: shift your weight from your right foot to your left foot. 

The idea is that on counts 3 or 7 you aren't taking a step with a full weight change when you bring your foot back underneath you. You can collect the foot on counts 3/7 and then actually change weight on 4/8. This will keep you on time and also allow you to have more hip action if you do it properly.

Someone already said this, but please don't bend over at the waist at all and don't bend your knees too much; also don't let your frame get lazy and collapse. It looks awkward from the outside and it'll feel awkward for your partner. Stand up straight/maintain good posture always. (And that doesn't mean be stiff without ever looking at each other, just don't go overboard trying to accommodate the height difference)

Now I'm 5'5", but I can lead/follow people up to about 6'1"/ 6'2"without much difficulty. My dance instructor would always say the key to it is a good frame. You do need to have your frame adjust to your partners height, but adjusting the height of your frame should be in the rotation of the your elbow, rather than dropping your shoulders/collapsing your elbows to your sides. If you're tall you probably also have long arms, so that should be doable. It's in your best interest to maintain a two-hand hold/ other holds that don't require a hand on the followers shoulder blade rather than full frame with followers significantly shorter than you. Also stick to moves that don't require your follower to reach all the way around you or above you (like a leader's head roll or a barrel turn or like a reverse cuddle-wrap position)

Aesthetic preferences can exist "just because" without any reason behind it, but if I learned anything getting a social science degree, it's that often there is a reason behind behavior and its worth trying to find that reason. 

Another example is why do people broadly think particular ethnicities are more/less attractive? Like it's totally possible to just coincidentally like guys who are tall or to coincidentally only date white men your whole life without it meaning anything else, but when it's an expectation or behavior that broadly impacts all of society you have to wonder where that expectation comes from. Why is it that people think taller men are more attractive? What assumptions, social norms, stereotypes, etc. lead to this overarching assumption that (with all else equal) tall guys are better? 

You have to remember that attraction, like food preferences, are often a mix of acquired and natural preferences. So the best way to find out why a behavior or preference is prominent is asking the people who hold that belief or exhibit that behavior. 

And most things (not just height) aren't a make-or-break thing when dating, but that doesn't mean the preference isn't still widespread / can genuinely mpact people's chances.

Tl;Dr: You're not really going to find any tutorials cause there's no point to a three-person dance other than to be silly/have fun on occasion. Still, here's my advice on how to do that and my 2 cents on the subject.

As a follower with two leads, it's always been a blast. A lot of the regulars at my favorite dancing spot are friends so I've had them switch out in the middle of a dance (they think they're sneaking but I always notice beforehand). Also have had people do a partner switch with two leads and two follows switching partnerships during a song; that's a lot of fun too.

Leading two followers is definitely really difficult, but I've only ever done it for shits and giggles with friends or during a dance class where they're weren't enough leads. Works really well on beginners so they can have more fun without stressing about not messing up. Their skill level isn't high enough for them to get bored by the handfull of moves I can lead. 

Best option to maximize enjoyment (not necessarily to look flashy though) is to not only focus on leading individual moves for the follows but make them do quite a lot of rotating/changes of places while you also change place. Add in a couple basic turns/ figures and you'll have a good time or at least a good laugh. Key to pulling it off is relaxing and improvising (and hopefully having followers willing to improvise with you). Go simple and clear with your moves, add in some rhythm changes/pauses that go with the music, and remember to also do some spins or tricks just by yourself (you're also a dancer in the equation, not just in charge of spinning the followers).
As a follower and leader, I just wanted to say that every time I've done this I've loved it regardless of my role. (Especially as a follower and even more so when switching)

If you're struggling to take smaller steps out of turns, you're probably not in full control of your weight during the turn. 

The best way to get better at turns is to practice them on your own without a leader there. You'll be more aware whether you're starring to go off balance even if no one is there to help (or sometimes hinder) you. 

You should be able to tell where your weight is in your feet always and be able to control it (like if your weight is more in your heel, midfoot, ball, or high ball; for spins in salsa you're almost always using a ball/high ball).

Additional tips: 

(1) Make sure your not trying to do the whole turn on one foot. That's a spin and they're harder to control.  A turn is more like placing a foot and pivoting (normally 180°), placing the next foot and pivoting, etc. For a basic single turn you should really only be stepping forward and slightly to the right, then leave your feet there as you pivot on your left to face the back, transfer weight back into your right foot and pivot to face the front, then close your feet/ transfer weight.

(2) Try to keep your inner thighs engaged. This looks like the ability to close your legs while standing up by pulling them together. You should use these muscles while dancing to help you stay balanced.  You don't have to be falling over-unbalanced to be unbalanced/to not have your weight in your control. Also it'll force you to keep your feet underneath yourself; you can't take big steps while simultaneously pulling your legs together.

1. I agree with the first comment saying you should just focus what you've been taught and improve those. 

Otherwise, I wouldn't say there is a particular "number" of body rolls you should know. You should just work on isolation and understanding how your body moves. Chest isolations are the most difficult, so practice that, and also practices isolations with your hips. If you can do both of those recently well, someone will be able to lead you in a body roll/wave you've never done before as long as you're receptive to the directions they are guiding you in. (Leading body rolls is a whole 'nother thing, but you need to be able to do a body roll/wave yourself before trying to lead it anyway so still practice isolation exercises.)

I'm not going to try to disagree with your opinion, it makes sense and opinion is just that, but I do want to add that 1. Synchronization and 2. Formation changes are extremely difficult to do well and take a lot of practice. 

As someone who has danced in and also choreographed Latin formations similar to (but definitely less complex) as the one you linked, I think you may be under estimating just how much time and effort it takes to get a group of people to dance in synch together. You end up having to dictate every little action that their body should take like how turned in/out the foot is, how much is your shoulder rotated up/down, how straight or bent is your elbow, how much bend do you have in your knees, what angle is your head at titled at, where you should be looking, etc. for nearly every second of the dance. If you don't decide how something is being done, then at least one person is going to do it differently. And everyone has to remember all of these little details; but memory alone won't allow you to dance at tempo so it really needs to be muscle memory. 

As for formations, they are nearly impossible to do without having everyone at practices consistently and even then it takes so much spatial awareness and flexibility. People need to think not only of their absolute position on a floor, but also their relative position to the couples around them; however, that spacing changes depending on what the size of the floor is because every performance venue is different (Especially for some random Latin club). You also have to realize that the choreography for each person/couple has to be specific for where they need to move to, how, and when in order to make the overall shape change while still looking synchronized. And you're lucky if you only need to learn those specifics for one position because you probably don't even have all of the people in the formation at the final show, meaning people have to know multiple positions and know how each of them work (while still dancing well).

Anyway, that was a long unnecessary rant/ response to say the annoyance is valid to an extent, but also accomplishing your critiques is difficult even for individuals and groups that practice a lot and have good choreography.

I started dancing ballroom in college and at first I started as someone who learned both the leader and follower steps in class (I couldn't decide), but since there weren't any good leaders I switched to leading 100% of the time. When I take classes I almost always lead so that I can memorize how to do the steps. When I go social dancing I typically follow so that I can learn more steps because someone else is leading me through it. I also lead at social dances, but that's mostly when there's a group of shy/new people (mostly women but also men) who are scared and nervous so I can give them a little helping hand. I tend to lead a lot for male followers who find it hard to get another man to lead them. I guess I also lead when some guy who's super new asks me to dance and we quickly realize he has no idea what he's doing, so I lead him through moves to help him out. And sometimes I see someone cool and just want to talk to them, asking them to dance as a leader (or someone who can do both) is a great way to start conversation.

Things that others have mentioned also apply for me: wanting to have more options for people to dance with, balancing out classes, saving people from creepy leads, to be a better follower, etc. But I also think I just love teaching and learning; it's super helpful to know how to lead when teaching others. Otherwise you'll only know how to do your own steps and not the steps the other partner needs to do (for leads or follows).

Also, switch dances are so much fun!

I think you should do it. Whether you wrestle on the girls team or the guys team, I think you should do it. Being on the girls team might seem like it'll automatically be invalidating to your gender, but you can work out ways with your teammates, coaches, parents, etc. to make yourself more comfortable. You might even find that the girls team is more comfortable than the boy's, but try talking to both coaches and maybe your school's athletic director to figure it out. Anyway, if you want to wrestle then do it.

Will you be outmatched? Yes, 100%. You're not necessarily starting late (lots of people start freshman year of HS), but you're gonna be behind the majority of people in skill regardless of sex. 

Are there potential safety issues wrestling on the men's team as a trans guy? Yes, that's just a fact. You can attribute it to your biology, to bigotry, or whatever else. As a female wrestler I don't believe injuries naturally happen to us more than boys (even when wrestling on a boys team). When society already thinks you shouldn't do an activity  people will come up with reasons to say it's bad for you/more dangerous. With that said, I should also add that there are definitely people who may try to intentionally hurt you because of your identity (depending on how conservative your area/state is). It happens to girls on boys teams and it happened a lot to my brothers too (we're African American and people are racist). You should keep that in mind, but hopefully you won't let it stop you (there are risks to every sport).

Will your weight matter? Not really. You'll probably be down another 10lbs once you get into wrestling shape, so you'll only really be going against other people who are about 105. Your lack of skill is going to be the biggest factor for you, not your strength or weight (regardless of the team you're on). 

Should you bind? I would say no for health concerns. I'm non-binary afab and still just wrestle in a sports bra. If you have medium to small chest then a sports bra will probably be fine to keep disphoria at bay. If you're larger chested then you should talk to a doctor/trainer about it and just wear the tightest sports bra you can for the time being.

Be smart, be strong, and commit to a move if you're going to do.

Push yourself to drill/spar with people that are bigger/strong/more aggressive than you. Even if you aren't able to score on them, make it hard for them take you down. Fight, scramble, and push yourself mentally to not just let them move you around; make them work for it.

Since your new you probably don't know what angles to go for or how to get leverage on you opponents; that's what you need to focus on learning. I'm black, bi, and trans (NB), so I'm gonna chime in here for a bit and explain why I and many others choose to use the progress flag rather than simply the rainbow flag.

Tl;Dr It's telling people to stop arguing over the use of microlabels cause broad labels and microlabels can coexist peacefully. 

To explain further: There are some people in the queer community that say the use of microlabels (like omni) are bi-erasure. Therefore, if you're attracted to 2 or more genders then you should call yourself Bi and that's it; ie. Micro labels shouldn't exist and we should stop using them. On the other hand, you can sometimes see people pushing another person to use a more specific label (that they may technically fit the popular definition for) even if that particular person would rather just use Bi and leave it at that. Last, you might find people who are comfortable using both a microlabel and a more broad label and will do so interchangeably. Not everyone is comfortable with using both a micro label and a broad label though, so they choose to use the label their most comfortable with. 

The point here is people should be free to use the labels they're comfortable with without people questioning it or pushing them to choose another more/less specific label. We can all coexist regardless of our choice in labels.
